Utility Non-Payment Risk & Consequence Model

Predicting electricity billing risk from real smart-meter data, and modeling what actually happens next

Hugo Garcia Moreno

August 21, 2026

1. What this project actually does

Most student “predict the bill” projects stop at forecasting a dollar amount. This one chains four pieces together:

[Real NYC weather] --> [Degree-day regression] --> [Predicted monthly bill]
                                                            |
                                                            v
[Real SGCC usage data] --> [Logistic reg. + tree] --> [ML risk tier] --> [Markov chain risk engine] --> [P(disconnected), E[months to disconnect]]
                                                                                   ^
                                                                                   |
                                                                    [HEFPA-cited consequence cascade]
  1. Statistically, can the pattern of a household’s or business’s electricity usage (the shape of it over time, separate from the dollar amount) predict whether they’re at elevated risk of a serious non-payment or billing problem? (Section 4.)
  2. Physically, how does a local weather record turn into a predicted monthly bill, and what does an actual heatwave do to it? (Section 5.)
  3. Stochastically, if a bill’s status is a state (current, late, severely late, disconnected), how does it move between those states over time, and how long does that take, as a function of risk tier and bill-to-income stress? (Section 6, a discrete-time Markov chain.)
  4. As a matter of policy, once a bill actually goes unpaid, what happens next, in calendar days and dollars? And where can available protections interrupt that sequence? (Section 7.)

Piece 1 is a machine-learning pipeline trained on individually labeled utility data. Piece 2 is a physical model (the same degree-day method utilities use for weather-normalized billing) run on historical NYC temperatures. Piece 3 is linear algebra, but where no public dataset exists to fit its inputs, those inputs are stated modeling assumptions, not measurements, and the report says so at the point each one is introduced. Piece 4 is a small rules engine built from actual New York State utility regulation, with each rule cited. These are kept in separate scripts on purpose. A statistical risk score, an assumed transition probability, and a legal deadline are three different kinds of claim, and blending them into one number would hide the distinctions a reader needs in order to trust or challenge any of this.

2. Data

dt <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "clean_wide.rds"))
features <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "features.rds"))
flag_tab <- table(dt$FLAG)

The consumption data is the public State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC) electricity-theft dataset: 33,840 real electricity customers, daily meter readings from 2014-01-01 to 2016-10-31, each labeled FLAG = 1 if the utility confirmed the account for electricity theft/billing fraud. It was released alongside a peer-reviewed paper:

Zheng, Z., Yang, Y., Niu, X., Dai, H.-N., & Zhou, Y. (2018). “Wide and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Electricity-Theft Detection to Secure Smart Grids.” IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics, 14(4), 1606-1615. https://doi.org/10.1109/TII.2017.2785963

Being precise about what FLAG means: this dataset labels confirmed electricity theft (meter tampering / bypass), which utilities treat as the most serious form of revenue loss from a customer relationship. It is not literally “this household missed a bill.” I’m using it as the closest publicly available, individually-labeled, real-world proxy for “this account’s usage behavior correlates with serious non-payment risk,” which is an honest and common substitution in this research area (there is no public dataset that labels ordinary missed payments at the individual level, for obvious privacy reasons). Section 5 returns to this limitation.

Class balance: 30225 normal accounts vs. 3615 flagged (10.7%). That imbalance is realistic for this kind of problem, and it drives the modeling choices in Section 4.

3. From a raw meter reading to a feature table

A theft or non-payment signal doesn’t live in any single day’s kWh reading. It lives in the shape of usage over time. Working straight off the 1034-day-wide raw matrix, I engineered 14 per-customer statistical features: overall level and volatility, the share of missing or exactly-zero reads, the longest gap in reporting, a linear trend over the whole series, weekday/weekend and winter/summer ratios, and year-over-year drift.

A real data-cleaning problem showed up immediately: a handful of accounts in this “residential” file report usage in the thousands of kWh/day (almost certainly commercial/industrial meters mixed into the file). Naive ratio features (weekend usage / weekday usage, winter / summer, 2016 usage / 2014 usage) blew up toward infinity whenever one of these accounts had a near-zero reading in the denominator period. For roughly 1% of accounts this wasn’t a rounding error, it was values in the thousands. The fix was to switch these three features from a raw ratio to a log-ratio (log1p(period A) - log1p(period B)): same “which period was higher, by roughly what multiple” information, but bounded and stable as usage approaches zero. range_ratio was left as a plain ratio but winsorized at the 1st/99th percentile. This is the kind of thing that looks like a footnote but actually determines whether a model is measuring signal or measuring an outlier. See scripts/02_feature_engineering.R for the full before/after.

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "feature_distributions.png"))

Distributions of four of the strongest features, split by outcome.

Flagged accounts show up as (a) noticeably higher day-to-day volatility once you control for scale, (b) more missing/zero reads and longer reporting gaps, and (c) a more pronounced upward drift in usage from 2014 to 2016, all patterns that make physical sense for a tampered meter that is used more freely over time and reported on less reliably.

4. Modeling non-payment/theft risk

mr <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "model_results.rds"))

Two models were trained on a 70/30 stratified split (10,136 held-out test customers): an interpretable logistic regression and a decision tree (rpart), both trained cost-sensitively to counter the ~89%/11% class imbalance: observations were weighted (logistic) or the tree’s split loss was penalized (decision tree) so that missing a true flagged account costs roughly 8.4x more than a false alarm, matching the actual class imbalance.

Why not just report accuracy? Because a model that predicts “not at risk” for every single customer would already score 89.3% accuracy here, while being completely useless, since it would flag zero of the real theft/non-payment cases. This is precisely the scenario precision/recall and ROC/AUC exist for.

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "roc_curves.png"))

ROC curves for both models against the no-skill diagonal.

Both models land at a respectable, believable AUC around 0.75, consistent with published results on this dataset using classical (non-deep-learning) features, and not suspiciously close to 1.0, which would be a red flag for leakage.

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "confusion_matrix.png"))

Confusion matrix at the Youden-optimal operating threshold.

At the Youden-optimal threshold the logistic model catches 69% of true flagged accounts (recall) while roughly 21% of everything it flags turns out to be a genuine positive (precision). That precision looks low in isolation, but it’s the right trade for this use case: a flag here should trigger low-cost proactive outreach (a payment-plan offer, a HEAP screening call) long before anything resembling an accusation, so the cost of a false positive is small and the cost of a false negative (missing a household headed for disconnection) is not.

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "coefficients.png"))

Standardized logistic regression coefficients.

The coefficients read the same story the density plots showed: usage volatility (log_sd_kwh, cv_kwh) and a longer history of missing reads are the strongest positive signals; a wide, stable, well-metered usage range (range_ratio) is the strongest protective signal.

5. Forecasting the bill from real weather

wthr <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "weather_results.rds"))

Everything above works from usage shape, not the bill amount. This section adds the missing piece: a real physical forecast of the bill itself, using the standard utility-industry degree-day method: electricity demand for heating and cooling scales with how far a day’s temperature sits from a 65°F “balance point,” not with temperature directly.

The temperature data is real: daily NYC-area records for all of 2015 (chosen to line up with the SGCC data’s own 2014-2016 window), from the public zonination/weather-us historical weather archive. The dollar calibration is externally anchored, not invented: the model’s cooling-season sensitivity is set so that a full Jun-Sep cooling season matches NEADA’s published 2026 Mid-Atlantic average summer cooling bill of $790, a real, cited, independent number the model is checked against, not fit to. Heating sensitivity is set at 40% of the cooling rate, a stated assumption (Northeast homes lean on gas heat, so the electric bill’s heating response is real but smaller) rather than a second anchored figure.

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "weather_bill_forecast.png"))

A full year of predicted bills from real NYC temperatures.

The weather-shock simulator

Real NYC heatwaves run 5-7 days with daily highs near 95-100°F. Swapping six days of the model’s hottest month (August) for a representative heatwave day (mean temp 90°F) and recomputing that month’s cooling degree-days raises the predicted bill from $300.13 to $327.74, a 9.2% jump from six unusual days. Section 6 carries this shock through to its actual consequence: the same dollar increase means very different things at different incomes.

6. A stochastic risk engine: the bill’s lifecycle as a Markov chain

markov <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "markov_results.rds"))

Sections 4-5 produce two numbers: an ML risk tier and a predicted bill. This section is what actually uses both of them together, by modeling a bill’s status explicitly as a state that moves over time. Four states, one month per step, aligned with the HEFPA timeline in Section 7 (a ~35-day notice-to-disconnection window is, for a monthly model, “about one step”):

Current → Late (1-30 days) → Severe (31-60+ days, disconnection-eligible) → Disconnected (absorbing in this model).

Two different kinds of input set the transition probabilities, and this report is explicit about which is which:

  • The Current → Late probability is grounded in the fitted classifier: it’s set by the same Low / Elevated / High risk tier from Section 4’s logistic model.
  • Once an account is late, whether it cures or progresses is set by a stated, illustrative function of “stress index” (predicted bill ÷ assumed monthly income): rising stress lowers the cure probability and raises the progress probability, clipped to valid probabilities. This function is a modeling assumption, not a measurement: no public dataset labels individual month-by-month delinquency transitions, so there is nothing to fit it to. Saying so here, rather than presenting illustrative numbers as empirical ones, is the entire point of keeping this section separate from Section 4.

All of the matrix algebra below (n-step transition matrices, the fundamental matrix, expected time to absorption) is implemented directly with base R linear algebra, solve() on I - Q, rather than a package call. I wanted this section to show the mechanics, not hide them behind a library.

kable(round(markov$illustrative_matrix, 3), caption = "Example transition matrix: Elevated risk, near-HEAP-eligible income, typical August bill")
Example transition matrix: Elevated risk, near-HEAP-eligible income, typical August bill
Current Late Severe Disconnected
Current 0.880 0.12 0.000 0.000
Late 0.483 0.17 0.347 0.000
Severe 0.203 0.00 0.553 0.243
Disconnected 0.000 0.00 0.000 1.000 
include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "markov_trajectory.png"))

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "markov_scenarios.png"))

The same 6-day heatwave, compared across risk tier and income.

Two things stand out. First, risk tier alone spans a huge range: at moderate income, a Low-risk account’s expected time to disconnection is measured in decades (27 years, so effectively not a near-term concern), while a High-risk account at the same income is measured in years. Second, and this is what the weather-shock simulator was built to show: the identical 6-day heatwave moves the 12-month disconnection probability by a larger absolute amount for the near-HEAP-eligible household than for the moderate-income one, in every risk tier. The same weather event hits different households differently. Climate-economics research describes this equity mechanism; here it comes out of a fully specified model a reader can inspect.

How much do the stated assumptions matter? A sensitivity analysis

The weakness of this chain, stated above, is that the transition probability functions for already-late accounts are assumptions rather than fitted values. The right response is to measure how much that matters: if the conclusions swung wildly whenever an assumed coefficient moved a little, the model would be decoration. So 09_sensitivity.R runs two checks on the reference scenario (Elevated tier, near-HEAP-eligible income, typical August bill).

sens <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "sensitivity_results.rds"))

One at a time. Each assumed parameter is moved ±20% from its stated value while the rest stay put:

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "sensitivity_tornado.png"))

Tornado analysis: each assumed parameter perturbed <U+00B1>20%, one at a time.

No single ±20% perturbation moves the 12-month disconnection probability by more than about ±0.03 around its stated-value run of 0.188. The most influential single parameter turns out to be the Elevated tier’s base slip probability, and that is the one input anchored to the fitted classifier’s operating thresholds rather than assumed. The model leans hardest on its best-grounded number, which is the right way around.

All at once. A joint Monte Carlo draws every assumed parameter simultaneously from independent ±20% ranges (1,932 valid draws of 2,000):

include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "sensitivity_montecarlo.png"))

Joint Monte Carlo: every assumed parameter drawn from a <U+00B1>20% range simultaneously.

Even with everything perturbed at once, 95% of outcomes stay between 0.133 and 0.253. The headline stays “roughly a one-in-five chance within a year” instead of flipping to negligible or near-certain. And the qualitative claim the project rests on, High risk above Elevated above Low at identical income and bill, holds in 100.0% of joint draws. The exact probabilities inherit the assumptions’ uncertainty. The ordering and the order of magnitude do not.

7. What happens after a bill actually goes unpaid

This section is not a statistical model, on purpose. Section 4 estimates a probability from usage data. This section states, as accurately as I could research it, what New York State utility regulation requires once a bill goes unpaid. Mixing the two, letting a risk score imply a legal timeline, would be a real error, so they’re built and presented separately.

cons <- readRDS(file.path(out_dir, "consequences.rds"))
kable(cons$cascade[, .(`Day (after due date)` = day_offset, Category = category, Event = event)])
Day (after due date) Category Event
0 billing Bill due; balance unpaid
20 notice Utility may issue a Final Termination Notice (HEFPA allows this starting 20 days after the due date) [1]
35 disconnection Earliest lawful disconnection date – HEFPA requires >=15 days’ notice after the Final Termination Notice [1]
35 fee A 1.5%/month late payment charge has been accruing on the unpaid balance since the due date [1]
NA protection Nov 1 - Apr 15 only: cold-weather protections apply – utility must attempt direct contact >=3 days before shutoff, and cannot disconnect for 15 business days after a required social-services referral, regardless of the day-35 date above [1]
35 fee If disconnected: service is restored once the account is resolved; a reconnection fee applies, set by the utility’s own tariff (commonly $20-$150+ for electric, more after-hours; NY does not publish one universal statewide amount) [3]
NA credit If the unpaid balance is referred to a third-party debt collector: THIS is the point (not the missed payment itself) at which it can appear on a credit report. New York utilities generally do not report routine on-time/late payment history to the three major credit bureaus themselves [2]

Primary sources:

  • NY Dept. of Public Service, “Your Rights as a Residential Gas, Electric or Steam Customer Under HEFPA” – https://dps.ny.gov/your-rights-residential-gas-electric-or-steam-customer-under-hefpa (15-day disconnection notice, 1.5%/month late fee, Nov 1-Apr 15 cold-weather protections, deferred payment agreement terms, security deposit rules)
  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, on utility bills and credit reports – https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/does-my-history-of-paying-utility-bills-like-telephone-cable-electricity-or-water-go-in-my-credit-report-en-1817/ (utilities generally do not report routine payment history to the major credit bureaus; a credit-report impact typically requires the debt to be referred to a third-party collection agency first)
  • UtilityExplained.com, reconnection fee ranges (a market survey, not a regulatory figure; reconnection fees are set by each utility’s own tariff)
  • NY OTDA HEAP guidelines (income tiers / benefit caps shown are illustrative and republished yearly. Verify current figures at mybenefits.ny.gov before relying on them for a real decision)
include_graphics(file.path(out_dir, "plots", "late_fee_projection.png"))

HEFPA’s 1.5%/month late charge, compounding on the outstanding balance.

The most important fact in this section, and one a usage-based ML model could never tell you: routine non-payment does not, by itself, damage a credit score. New York utilities generally don’t report ordinary payment history to the major bureaus at all. The credit consequence only attaches at a specific, later, avoidable step: referral to a third-party collection agency. That is the kind of fact that should reach a household before day 35, not after.

Turning a risk score into a recommended action

kable(cons$examples[, .(Scenario = scenario, `Risk score` = round(risk_prob, 3), Tier = tier, `Recommended action` = action)])
Scenario Risk score Tier Recommended action
Low risk 0.050 Low No action beyond a normal reminder.
Elevated risk 0.493 Elevated Proactive outreach recommended: payment plan (DPA) offer + HEAP screening before day 20.
High risk 0.838 High Priority outreach before Final Termination Notice window; DPA + HEAP screening + cold-weather protection check.

This is where Sections 4 and 5 connect, without collapsing into each other: the ML model’s output sets when to intervene; HEFPA and HEAP set what the intervention actually offers.

8. Limitations

  • The label is a proxy. FLAG marks confirmed electricity theft, not garden-variety late payment. The overlap is real (both are forms of revenue loss the utility responds to) but not exact, and I’m not claiming otherwise.
  • The consequence figures are New York-specific and time-bound. HEFPA is a New York State law; other states have different (sometimes much weaker) protections. The HEAP numbers are one program-year’s guidance and change annually.
  • Reconnection fees are not a single number. They’re set utility-by-utility by tariff; the range shown is a market survey, not a rule.
  • ~26% of readings in the raw data are missing, and missingness itself turned out to be predictive (see Section 3). Some of what the model learns is really “how well-monitored is this account,” not purely “how much electricity did it use.”
  • AUC ~0.75 is good, not great. There’s real room for improvement, for example neighborhood or weather covariates, or the CNN approach from the original paper. That open room is part of why this is a project and not a solved problem.
  • The weather module and the usage-risk model are not paired to the same customers. The SGCC data is Chinese and unlabeled by location; the weather data is NYC history. They’re joined only through the shared 2014-2016 time window and through the Markov chain’s stated income and tier inputs, and I don’t claim they describe the same households.
  • The Markov transition probabilities are assumptions, not measurements. Section 6 states this at the point of introduction, and it’s repeated here because it’s the easiest thing in this project to misread as more empirical than it is. What’s real inside that section: the four-state structure mirroring HEFPA’s actual timeline, the risk tiers from a fitted model, and the linear algebra connecting them. The sensitivity analysis at the end of Section 6 quantifies how much this limitation matters: ±20% perturbations of every assumed coefficient, singly and jointly, leave the headline probability in the same band and the tier ordering intact in 100% of draws.
  • Disconnection is treated as absorbing. Real accounts do get reconnected; modeling it as a permanent absorbing state is a standard simplification for this kind of analysis, not a claim that reconnection is impossible.

9. Reproducing this

All code lives in scripts/01 through scripts/09, run in order, from a plain R installation (data.table, ggplot2, rpart, rmarkdown, knitr – no paid APIs required; 01-05 need the raw SGCC CSV in data/data.csv and 06-09 need the NYC weather CSV already included at data/weather/nyc_weather_raw.csv). See the top-level README.md for the exact dataset download link and citation.
